title: Missions Require Marketing
hook: A clean terminal window means little if no rare-disease researcher ever sees Graham's tool.
counterintuition: Marketing is not vanity once the work has proof, but the distribution that lets the right audience test, use, and amplify it.
tryThisNow: Write the smallest public artifact your mission needs next: a demo, memo, field note, talk, page, or invitation for one real audience.
keyTakeaway: Missions require marketing because clarified work needs visibility with the right audience before it can gather allies, pressure, proof, and reach.

breakdown.fastRead:
You see Graham's terminal window with clean output after months of rare-disease tooling work. The script works on the test data. The mission is real enough to help. No researcher knows it exists.

He writes one public artifact: a short open lab note for the small group that maintains the relevant dataset.

A mission that stays invisible cannot gather the allies, pressure, or proof that make it larger than private intent. Marketing is not decoration here. It is how useful work becomes findable.
breakdown.deepRead:
It took Ian three dawn pickups to see that his food rescue routing pilot had become more than a private efficiency trick. Bakery crates sat in the van before sunrise, and the route change got surplus bread to two shelters before breakfast. He wanted to keep improving quietly because publicity felt like self-promotion. The decision is whether to hide the evidence or create one artifact the right people can use: a one-page route note for bakeries, shelter coordinators, and the volunteer dispatch desk.

Visibility is not vanity when it lets the right people act.

Marketing becomes cheap when it is detached from proof. It becomes useful when proven work needs an audience. The question is not, "How do I make myself look important?" The question is, "Who needs to see this so the mission can grow stronger, more tested, or more useful?"

The demo video timeline glows in a quiet coworking room while Neil edits an accessibility plugin walkthrough. Before, he treated the plugin as successful because his own test page passed. After three users with low vision tried it, he understood the marketing task differently. The public artifact should not be a triumphant launch thread. It should be a two-minute demo for maintainers of small civic websites, showing the exact barrier fixed and the installation step they can try.
breakdown.fullRead:
What should become visible next, and to whom?

Brian asks that while a red heat map sits beside a fan-delivery list at the community center. His heat-risk alert system worked for one apartment block during a hot week. His prediction is that a broad social post will create momentum. The reveal is that the right audience is narrower: building managers, tenant organizers, and the clinic nurse who already checks on older residents. He is about to decide between chasing attention and producing a one-page field note that shows who received alerts, who needed fans, and which hallway stayed dangerously hot.

Marketing is the work of making useful proof findable by the people who can use it.

That is why marketing comes after support and little bets. If the mission is still only a slogan, marketing becomes noise. If the mission has evidence, marketing becomes a bridge. It connects the work to people who can test it, use it, fund it, criticize it, join it, or carry it farther than one person can.

Metal shavings collect around Adrian's fixture after a week of apprenticeship demonstrations. He wants more young machinists to see that fixture setup is a craft worth mastering. The easy version of marketing would be a glossy portfolio about his talent. He hovers over that idea, then builds a different artifact: three annotated photos showing common fixture mistakes, plus a note for two trade instructors who place apprentices. The audience can act on that proof.

There is a discipline to this. Do not market everything. Do not shout to everyone. Choose the public artifact that matches the mission's next need. A demo if people need to see the work operate. A memo if decision-makers need a concise case. A field note if peers need evidence from reality. A talk if the right community gathers in one room. A page if the work needs a stable home.

"Can tenants read it before court?" Aaron asks, eviction notice under a scanner lid. His postmortem on the legal-rights explainer is direct. The first version was accurate and invisible. The people who needed it did not visit the legal aid website before hearings. Marketing does not mean making Aaron famous. It means placing a one-page explainer where tenant organizers, library staff, and court volunteers can hand it to someone at the right moment.

Marketing also creates accountability. Once the artifact is public, the mission can be tested by people outside your own head. They may ignore it, share it, correct it, improve it, or reveal that the next audience is different. That response is not separate from the mission. It is how the mission gathers force.

Private intent can be sincere and still have no public effect. If the work has capital, a frontier, and small-bet evidence, hiding it becomes its own failure mode. Make the proof visible to the audience that can act. Then let their response decide what the mission needs next.

questions.prompt: A researcher builds a useful rare-disease tool but keeps it private because publicity feels vain. What does mission marketing require?
choices: A broad personal-brand campaign.
A public artifact for the specific researchers or maintainers who can test and use the tool.
More private polishing until no one can criticize it.
questions.explanation: Marketing is visibility for useful proof. A targeted lab note lets the right people act, while broad branding and endless polishing miss the mission need.

questions.prompt: A food rescue pilot gets bread to shelters earlier, but only one volunteer knows the route. Which artifact would best create public force for the mission?
choices: A route note for bakeries, shelter coordinators, and dispatch volunteers showing timing and join points.
A flattering profile of the volunteer's dedication.
A private spreadsheet no partner can see.
questions.explanation: The route note makes the evidence usable by partners. The point is not praise for the volunteer; it is helping others extend the working pilot.

questions.prompt: An accessibility plugin works on tests, but maintainers keep asking what barrier it fixes and how to install it. What should the creator make visible?
choices: A vague announcement that accessibility matters.
A two-minute demo showing the broken state, the fix, and the install step.
Nothing, because good work should spread without explanation.
questions.explanation: The demo answers the audience's action question. Visibility should make adoption easier, not merely announce that the mission is worthy.

questions.prompt: A heat-risk alert pilot works on one apartment block. A broad social post may get likes, but building managers and clinic staff can act directly. What marketing choice fits the mission?
choices: Send a field note to the people who can change check-ins, fan delivery, or building response.
Post broadly and treat likes as the main signal.
Keep the pilot quiet because community health should never be marketed.
questions.explanation: The field note targets the audience with power to act. Likes may create attention, but the mission needs useful response and amplification.

questions.prompt: A craft mentor wants apprentices to learn fixture setup. Which artifact is better mission marketing than a glossy portfolio?
choices: A stylish page with no teaching details.
A private folder of demonstrations.
Three annotated mistake photos sent to trade instructors who can use them in class.
questions.explanation: The annotated photos serve a real audience and make the proof teachable. A glossy page may promote the mentor without advancing the mission.

questions.prompt: A legal-rights explainer is accurate but hidden on a website tenants rarely visit before court. What should the next marketing move solve?
choices: How to place a short artifact where tenant organizers, library staff, or court volunteers can hand it to people in time.
How to make the project lead seem more impressive.
How to add more legal detail without changing distribution.
questions.explanation: The mission problem is distribution at the moment of need. More detail or project-lead status will not help if tenants never see the explainer.

questions.prompt: A project lead says marketing is always empty self-promotion, so useful mission work should stay quiet. What correction best fits this idea?
choices: Marketing is only useful when it goes viral.
Targeted visibility can let the right people test, use, correct, or amplify proven work.
Private intent is always enough for public effect.
questions.explanation: The correction distinguishes visibility from vanity. Mission marketing is about connecting evidence with an audience that can act on it.

questions.prompt: Two mission teams have evidence. One sends a concise memo to the exact agency that can adopt the pilot. The other posts a vague inspirational thread to a broad audience. Which has better marketing discipline?
choices: The vague thread, because broad reach is always the goal.
The agency memo, because the artifact fits the audience that can act.
Neither, because missions should avoid public artifacts.
questions.explanation: The memo is better matched to the mission's next need. Reach matters only when it reaches people who can test, use, or amplify the work.

questions.prompt: A team releases many public posts before any little-bet evidence exists. The posts sound polished but cannot point to a tested result. What is the risk?
choices: Marketing has outrun proof and may become noise rather than mission support.
The team is guaranteed to succeed because visibility came early.
Evidence does not matter once public attention starts.
questions.explanation: Marketing works best after evidence exists. Without proof, visibility can become performance rather than a bridge between useful work and the right audience.

reviewCards.back: A mission needs visibility with the right audience so useful proof can be tested, used, corrected, amplified, or funded.

reviewCards.front: How is mission marketing different from vanity?
reviewCards.back: Vanity tries to make the person look important. Mission marketing makes proven work findable by people who can act on it.

reviewCards.front: What should decide the public artifact you create?
reviewCards.back: The mission's next audience and next need should decide: demo, memo, field note, talk, page, or invitation.

reviewCards.front: When is broad reach the wrong marketing goal?
reviewCards.back: Broad reach is weak when a specific audience can use the work. Reach should be judged by action, not raw attention.

reviewCards.front: Why should marketing usually follow evidence?
reviewCards.back: Evidence gives visibility something real to carry. Without tested work, marketing can become noise or personal branding.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Make mission evidence visible to the right audience. The skill is choosing the smallest public artifact that lets useful work be tested, used, corrected, or amplified.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a tool or method works in a small test, then create a demo or note for the people who can try it next.
If a local pilot worked, then write a field note for partners who can extend, fund, or challenge it.
If the mission involves teaching, then make one artifact instructors or peers can reuse immediately.
If the right people are not seeing the work, then move the artifact into their actual path instead of adding polish elsewhere.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, choose one mission artifact and one real audience. Write the title, format, audience, and the action you want that audience to take.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, make one piece of mission evidence more findable. Track action from the right audience, not general attention.
